summary: A small square wooden tower on Lake Huron south of Southampton, Ontario, built in 1877 as the rear of a harbour range, moved in 1901, and out of service since 1989.

access.note: Site and tower closed; no public access. The tower sits among private homes; the sources say it is best seen from the water, with a distant view from Chantry Island.

events.note: Constructed 1877 as part of the Southampton harbour improvements (Parks Canada); LighthouseFriends says the range was built in 1876
Rear range light put in operation on 5 May 1877 (LighthouseFriends, quoting the Department of Marine)
Rear tower moved 1,800 feet to McNab Point from the north side of Horseshoe Bay
Deactivated around 1970 (Parks Canada); LighthouseFriends has the rear light still called Southampton Harbour Light until at least 1971
Reactivated in 1974 as McNab Point Light (LighthouseFriends, Lighthouse Directory); Parks Canada gives c.1980
Light reactivated and automated around 1980 (Parks Canada)
Coast Guard covered the tower with white aluminium siding, which trapped moisture and let the wood rot; Parks Canada gives 1989
Marine Heritage Society removed the siding and put new cedar shingles on the tower
Designated a heritage lighthouse on 3 August 2012 (Parks Canada statement, report 2011-LR-009)

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Parks Canada gives 1877 as the year of construction. LighthouseFriends says the range was built in 1876 and its lights were first shown on 5 May 1877. The record's 1877 is kept for the tower.

The 1901 Chief Engineer's report says the back light moved 1,800 feet south-west onto a gravel ridge on the main shore, without naming McNab Point. LighthouseFriends gives 1,800 feet across Horseshoe Bay to McNab Point, and Parks Canada gives the move from the northern tip of Horseshoe Bay to McNab Point. Read together, they describe the same move.

notes_for_editor: Dates: reactivation 1974 (LighthouseFriends, Lighthouse Directory) against c.1980 (Parks Canada); siding 1988 (LighthouseFriends, Directory) against 1989 (Parks Canada); deactivation c.1970 (Parks Canada) against 'Southampton Harbour Light until at least 1971' (LighthouseFriends). The story states all of these. James Brown on the 1906 keeper list was matched by OCR line and checked on the page image (scan p.172, printed p.163). Cascaden, Lee and Buckley rest on LighthouseFriends alone; the 1877 to 1899 keepers are unchecked because the Canadian Marine reports in the corpus begin with the fiscal year ended 30 June 1900. Duncan McGregor Lambert kept Chantry Island and looked after the front light at the breakwater, a different structure, so he is named in the story but not on this roster. The Marine Heritage Society page on the 'Rear Range Light' restoration concerns the Saugeen River rear range (Parks Canada dates it to 1903), not McNab Point, so it was not used. The Directory's 'By 2026 it was severely detriorated' note is in the cached copy and is now used. LighthouseFriends prints $1.39 for the 1901 move; the 1901 Chief Engineer's report gives the removal cost as $139, so LighthouseFriends is a typo and the cost is left out. The 1901 report was read in full and does not name McNab Point. The 1901 move's distance comes from the 1901 report and LighthouseFriends; Parks Canada gives no distance. The record's access 'closed' agrees with both secondary sources. Five chapters for moderate evidence (the guide asks for 2 to 4); left for the editor. No newspaper search was run; Chronicling America is unlikely to hold Ontario local papers for this station. The story is about 900 words, below the 1,200 floor for rich evidence; it was not padded to reach it.
